extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties in TTAB/trademark inter partes proceedings (litigators before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules for disclosures, expert testimony disclosure, and the scope and limits of discovery in TTAB proceedings (based on Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 and related TTAB/37 CFR provisions). Intended to guide parties and counsel on what must be disclosed, timing, form, limitations, and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert disclosure — general requirement (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must disclose to the other parties the identity of any witness it may use at trial to present evidence under Federal Rule of Evidence 702, 703, or 705.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure obligation applies in addition to Rule 26(a)(1). Parties are not required to disclose consulting experts. The extent of the expert disclosure obligation is governed by Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2). Disclosure of planned or possible expert testimony must be made by the expert disclosure deadline regardless of whether other parties have made such disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written report requirement for retained/specially employed experts (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise stipulated or ordered, if the witness is retained or specially employed to provide expert testimony or is an employee whose duties regularly involve giving expert testimony, the disclosure must be accompanied by a written report prepared and signed by the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report must contain: (i) a complete statement of all opinions and the basis and reasons for them; (ii) the facts or data considered; (iii) any exhibits to be used to summarize or support them; (iv) the witness's qualifications, including publications in the previous 10 years; (v) a list of other cases in which the witness testified as an expert in the previous 4 years; and (vi) a statement of compensation to be paid for the study and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure content for witnesses who do not provide a written report (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness is not required to provide a written report, the disclosure must state the subject matter on which the witness is expected to present evidence and a summary of the facts and opinions to which the witness is expected to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary need not be as detailed as a full written report but must sufficiently inform adverse parties of the subject matter and expected testimony so they can plan discovery and any rebuttal experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for expert disclosures (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures must be made at the times and in the sequence that the court orders. Absent an order or stipulation, disclosures must be made: (i) at least 90 days before trial or when the case is ready for trial; or (ii) within 30 days after another party's disclosure if intended solely to contradict or rebut that party's expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In TTAB practice, expert disclosure is generally due 30 days prior to the close of discovery (or any deadline reset by Board order). If an expert is retained after the deadline, the party must promptly file a motion for leave to use expert testimony. Prompt post-deadline disclosure does not guarantee admissibility; the Board decides late identifications case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to supplement expert disclosures (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must supplement disclosures when required under Rule 26(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should revisit discussions about experts whenever it appears a testifying expert may become involved. See TBMP § 408.03 for duty-to-supplement details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to the Board about expert disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party disclosing plans to use an expert must notify the Board that it has made the required disclosure (but should not file with the Board the materials provided to adverse parties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification allows the Board to consider suspending proceedings for expert-related discovery. Failure to notify the Board is not necessarily a ground to exclude testimony; in some cases notification may not be necessary if expert-related discovery can be concluded by the close of discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board authority to suspend or set deadlines for expert discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon disclosure of plans to use expert testimony the Board may issue an order regarding expert discovery and/or set a deadline for any other party to disclose plans to use a rebuttal expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A suspension order may leave unchanged or reset existing Federal Rule deadlines for rebuttal expert disclosures. The Board may or may not suspend unrelated discovery activities depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for leave to use expert witness after disclosure deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expert is retained after the deadline for disclosure of expert testimony, the party must promptly file a motion for leave to use the expert's testimony at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with prompt motion and disclosure, the Board will evaluate late identification and may exclude the testimony; determinations are case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of disclosure obligations (37 CFR § 2.120(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure deadlines and obligations may be modified upon written stipulation of the parties approved by the Board, or upon motion granted by the Board, or by order of the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a stipulation or motion for modification is denied, deadlines and obligations may remain as originally set. Parties may agree to waive or modify initial disclosure obligations but must inform the Board by written stipulation or motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of disclosures — writing, signature, service (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(4) and 26(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the court orders otherwise, all Rule 26(a) disclosures must be in writing, signed, and served. Every disclosure and every discovery request, response, or objection must be signed by at least one attorney of record (or party, if unrepresented) and must state the signer's address, e-mail address, and telephone number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature constitutes certification that, after reasonable inquiry, the disclosure is complete and correct as of the time made. Unsigned disclosures may be stricken; other parties need not act on an unsigned disclosure until signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature certification standards for discovery requests/responses/objections (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief formed after reasonable inquiry, with respect to a discovery request, response, or objection: (i) it is consistent with the rules and warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument to change law; (ii) it is not interposed for any improper purpose such as harassment or delay; and (iii) it is neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome, considering the needs of the case, prior discovery, the amount in controversy, and importance of the issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of Rule 26(g) may have consequences; see TBMP § 408.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of discovery (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense, including documents, tangible things, and identity/location of persons having knowledge of discoverable matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant information need not be admissible at trial if discovery appears reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. Discovery may be taken as to matters not specifically raised in pleadings and to matters that might serve as the basis for additional claims or defenses, but parties must avoid 'fishing expeditions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on discovery — undue burden, cumulative/duplicative, proportionality (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: Even relevant discovery may be limited or denied if it is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, unduly burdensome, obtainable from a more convenient source, or if the harm to the person from whom discovery is sought outweighs the need of the requester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may permit a responding party to provide representative sampling or reduced information where full compliance would be unduly burdensome. Considerations include needs of the case, amount in controversy, parties' resources, and importance of issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI accessibility and production limits (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party need not provide discovery of electronically stored information (ESI) from sources it identifies as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost. The resisting party must show lack of reasonable accessibility; if shown, the requesting party must show good cause for production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing good cause, the Board will consider whether the discovery is cumulative, whether the requesting party had ample opportunity to obtain the information, and whether burden/expense outweighs likely benefit. Given the Board's limited jurisdiction and narrow issues, e-discovery burdens weigh heavily against production in most cases; parties should be precise and limit expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege and work-product protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileged information and attorney work product are exempt from discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting privilege, a party must describe the nature of withheld information per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5). Documents prepared in anticipation of litigation are discoverable only upon a showing of substantial need and inability to obtain the substantial equivalent without undue hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders and confidential commercial information
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of confidential commercial information is subject to the Board’s standard protective order or an approved substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For proceedings commenced or pending on or after August 31, 2007, the Board’s standard protective order automatically applies unless parties agree to and the Board approves a substitute. Protective orders may limit disclosure of customer names and other sensitive information, revealing only classes or subject to counsel-only access as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to hold discovery conference and required topics (Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must hold a discovery conference discussing the subjects set forth in Rule 26(f) and the nature and basis of claims and defenses, possibility of settlement or modification of pleadings, plans for disclosures and discovery, and any other subjects the Board may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are free to discuss additional topics to promote settlement or efficient adjudication. Because parties may stipulate to alter disclosure obligations, they should continue to discuss reciprocal obligations and progress even after the conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to make initial disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that has not made initial disclosures may not serve discovery requests or file a motion for summary judgment (except on Board jurisdiction or preclusion), and is precluded from filing a motion to compel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement of service of initial disclosures cannot be waived under these circumstances. If a party fails to make required or adequate disclosures, it may face motions to compel and sanctions, including possible judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number/length of depositions and requests
rubrics_metrics.description: By order, the court/Board may alter rule limits on the number of depositions and interrogatories or the length of depositions under Rule 30; by order or local rule, the court may limit requests under Rule 36.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may also stipulate to limits or agree to alternative arrangements to reduce cost and time; however, the Board may issue orders altering default limits where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith and proportionality obligations in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party has a duty to make a good faith effort to satisfy the discovery needs of its adversary and to seek only discovery proper and relevant to the issues in the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Rule 26(g) certifications attach responsibility for the reasonableness and purpose of discovery, a party ordinarily cannot argue a request is proper when propounded by itself but improper when propounded by its adversary, absent persuasive reasons. See TBMP §§ 408.01 and 414 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on motions to compel expanding scope beyond original requests
rubrics_metrics.description: A party will not be permitted, through a motion to compel, to obtain discovery broader in scope than that actually sought in the underlying discovery request(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to compel addresses compliance with a specific request; it cannot be used to expand the scope of what was originally requested.
